newsitem.title: USA: Dollar opens higher in U.S. trading.
newsitem.headline: Dollar opens higher in U.S. trading.

text.p: The dollar opened higher in U.S. trading Wednesday, resuming its upward march after a pause in reaction to leading industrial nations' attempts to hold down the surging currency.

The dollar surged on overseas markets, reaching a 34-month high against the German mark, before setting back when German and Japanese financial officials made remarks intended to cap the dollar's gains.

In an official statement from the German central bank, chief spokesman Manfred Koerber insisted the bank supports the latest statement by the Group of Seven major powers that said the dollar has gained sufficient value to be at parity with other major currencies.
Separately, Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka warned that Japan will take appropriate actions to tackle any excessive moves in the foreign exchange market.
Analysts said the Bundesbank had probably capped the dollar for the day, but said the rally still had further to run.

"I think the general bullishness in the market will prevail at least until the dollar reaches a level where these guys agree that they need to intervene," said Bill Bertha, chief dealer at Mellon Bank N.A. "(But) I think we're probably a ways from that."
The dollar opened in U.S. trading at 1.6829 marks, up from 1.6768 marks at Tuesday's close, and 123.85 yen, up from 123.26 yen.
In overseas trading, the dollar had reached a 34-month high of 1.6935 marks and a four-year high of 124.48 yen before retreating.
Analysts said the response to the Bundesbank statement was symptomatic of a market on tenterhooks for intervention.
"Whenever you see a big move there's going to be sensitivity, but it's just a case of wait and see," said Brian Hilliard, chief economist at Societe Generale Strauss Turnbull.
Analysts felt concerted intervention at current levels was unlikely, but did not rule out unilateral Japanese action.
"Very near-term it could be that the Japanese finally lose patience and decide to do something themselves," said Nigel Richardson, international economist at Yamaichi.
Japan's Ministry of Finance fuelled such fears on Wednesday, saying Japan would "take appropriate measures to tackle any excessive moves" in the foriegn exchange markets.

Economists said the beneficial effects of yen weakness were wearing off and rising import costs were dampening the profitability of other sectors of the Japanese economy. Germany and the United States had little interest in selling dollars, they said.

U.S. January retail sales and producer price data due Thursday and Friday should exacerbate the woes of the yen and, in particular, the mark as they highlight the health of the U.S. economy compared with those of Germany and Japan, analysts said.
